mainTopic: Whether a minor acquires through his חצר, and the rule that an unguarded field acquires for its owner only when he stands beside it.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a question from the page before: why do אבא כהן ברדלא and רבי ינאי disagree about whether a minor acquires through his חצר? The גמרא gives three answers. The first is that they argue whether we learn מציאה from גט. The second is that they argue whether a קטן is learned from a קטנה. The third is that there is no argument at all. Then a new משנה teaches that a person's field acquires an ownerless animal for him only if the animal cannot escape, like a deer with a broken leg or baby birds that cannot fly. שמואל adds that this works only when the owner is standing next to his field. The גמרא explains that a guarded חצר acquires even without the owner knowing, but an open, unguarded field acquires only when he is beside it. It proves this from a ברייתא about a forgotten sheaf (שכחה) and defends the proof through a back-and-forth over words in the פסוק. רב אשי settles it with the word 'יִהְיֶה'. עולא and רבה בר בר חנה agree with שמואל, and רבי אבא begins challenging עולא from a story about רבן גמליאל on a ship. That challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: First answer: can we learn found objects from divorce?
steps.stepSummary: One opinion learns the rules of מציאה from the rules of גט, and the other does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds that we learn the law of a found object from the law of a divorce document. The other Sage holds that we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its first answer to the question "what are they arguing about?" The argument comes down to whether we may learn מציאה from גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman can receive her גט through her חצר, even a קטנה. The one who says a minor has a חצר copies that rule over to found objects. The one who says a minor has no חצר refuses to copy it, so for a minor's מציאה the חצר does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: We learn (one law from another)
A found object (ownerless item someone picks up)
A divorce document
One Sage holds

steps.confusionAlert: This line starts in the middle of a sentence. The first "מר סבר" ("one Sage holds") is on the page before, so the opening words here are the end of that Sage's view.

phrases.english: we learn a found object from a divorce document,
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence that began on the previous page with "one Sage holds...". This is the view that a minor does have a חצר.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: לָא יָלְפִינַן מְצִיאָה מִגֵּט.
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: we do not learn a found object from a divorce document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from the previous page about what the two opinions argue over.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument is whether the rule of חצר for a גט can be applied to מציאה.

steps.title: Second answer: everyone agrees about a girl, they argue about a boy
steps.stepSummary: Everyone learns מציאה from גט for a קטנה. They only argue whether a קטן can be learned from a קטנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, say this: for a minor girl, everyone agrees that we learn found objects from divorce. They argue about a minor boy. One Sage holds that we learn the boy from the girl. The other Sage holds that we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to explain the argument. It moves the disagreement to a different spot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first answer the argument was about learning מציאה from גט. Now both sides accept that, but only for a קטנה, since a גט is only given to a girl. The new question is whether a קטן is treated like a קטנה. If he is, he also has a חצר. If he is not, he does not.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (another way to explain)
A minor girl
A minor boy
Everyone agrees
They argue

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that one argument can sit at different levels. It can be about learning one area of law from another, or about learning one person from another.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
regarding a minor girl, everyone agrees
that we learn a found object from a divorce document.
And here they argue about a minor boy:
One Sage holds: we learn a minor boy from a minor girl.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: לָא יָלְפִינַן קָטָן מִקְּטַנָּה.
phrases.english: And the other Sage holds: we do not learn a minor boy from a minor girl.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second explanation that moves the argument from גט-to-מציאה over to קטנה-to-קטן.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Everyone agrees a קטנה acquires מציאה through her חצר. The argument is only whether a קטן is learned from her.

steps.title: Third answer: no argument at all
steps.stepSummary: Each Sage spoke about a different case, so they do not really disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, say this: one Sage said one thing and the other Sage said another thing, and they do not argue.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third explanation: the two statements do not conflict at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who said a minor has a חצר was talking about receiving a גט. The one who said a minor has no חצר was talking about a מציאה. Since they spoke about two separate cases, both can be right.

keyTerms.meaning: One Sage said one thing (about one case)
And they do not disagree

steps.whatToRemember: There are three ways to read the argument: (1) whether we learn מציאה from גט, (2) everyone learns it for a קטנה and they argue about a קטן, (3) no argument, because one spoke about גט and the other about מציאה.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: מָר אֲמַר חֲדָא, וּמָר אֲמַר חֲדָא
phrases.english: one Sage said one thing, and the other Sage said another thing,
phrases.notes: The one who said a minor has a חצר meant for a גט. The one who said no meant for a found object.

phrases.english: and they do not disagree.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: מָר אֲמַר חֲדָא, וּמָר אֲמַר חֲדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the two earlier answers by removing the argument completely.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two statements are about different cases, גט and מציאה, so they do not conflict.

steps.title: A field acquires an animal only if it cannot escape
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if a person's field holds a crippled deer or baby birds that cannot fly, and he says 'my field acquired for me,' he acquires them. If the deer runs normally or the birds can fly, his words mean nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone saw people running after an ownerless animal, like a deer with a broken leg or baby birds that cannot fly yet, and he said 'My field has acquired it for me,' it is his. But if the deer was running normally, or the birds could already fly, and he said 'My field has acquired it for me,' he has said nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches when a person's field can grab ownership of an ownerless animal that is inside it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A field acquires only things that stay in it. A broken deer or baby birds that cannot fly are as good as trapped, so the field holds them. A healthy deer or flying birds can leave at any moment, so the field cannot hold them and his statement does nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: A found, ownerless item
A deer with a broken leg that cannot run away
Baby birds that have not yet learned to fly
'My field has acquired it for me'
He said nothing, meaning his words have no legal effect

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole idea of קנין חצר: a person's property can act like his hand and acquire things for him, but only things that will stay there.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
He saw people running after a found item,
after a deer with a broken leg,
after young birds that have not yet learned to fly,
and he said: "My field has acquired it for me". It has acquired it for him.
If the deer was running in its normal way,
or the young birds were flying,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: ״זָכְתָה לִי שָׂדִי״ – לֹא אָמַר כְּלוּם.
phrases.english: and he said: "My field has acquired it for me". He has said nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, moving from the earlier discussion of מציאה and גט to acquiring through one's field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A field acquires an ownerless animal for its owner only when the animal cannot leave on its own.

steps.title: The owner must be standing next to his field
steps.stepSummary: שמואל limits the משנה: the field acquires only when the owner is standing beside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: This only works when the owner is standing next to his field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings שמואל, who adds a condition to the משנה. The field acquires the animal only if its owner is standing next to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה did not mention where the owner was. שמואל adds a new requirement: the owner's presence beside the field. The next step will ask why this is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And that is only when...', a phrase that adds a condition to a ruling
Next to his field

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
And that is only when he is standing next to his field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: וְהוּא שֶׁעוֹמֵד בְּצַד שָׂדֵהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting condition to the משנה's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A field acquires for its owner only when he stands next to it.

steps.title: A courtyard acquires even without the owner knowing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל using רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, who says a person's חצר acquires for him even without his knowledge. So why must he stand beside it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But his field should acquire for him anyway! After all, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: A person's courtyard acquires for him even without his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on שמואל. If a חצר can acquire for a person who does not even know about the item, why should he need to stand next to it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule shows that a חצר works on its own, without the owner being aware. If knowing is not needed, being physically present should not be needed either. That seems to make שמואל's condition unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But let it acquire for him!', the opening of a challenge
A person's courtyard or property
Without his knowledge

phrases.english: But let his field acquire for him anyway,
as Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲצֵרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם קוֹנָה לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ!
phrases.english: A person's courtyard acquires for him even without his knowledge!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's condition from step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's requirement that the owner stand next to his field
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a חצר acquires even without the owner's knowledge, his presence beside it should not matter.

steps.title: Guarded versus unguarded courtyards
steps.stepSummary: The rule of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא applies only to a guarded courtyard. An unguarded field, like an open field, acquires only when the owner stands next to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule is only about a guarded courtyard. But a courtyard that is not guarded acquires for him if he is standing next to his field, and if he is not, it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there are two kinds of חצר. A guarded one acquires on its own, even without the owner knowing. An unguarded one acquires only if the owner is standing next to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule was about a secured courtyard (חצר המשתמרת), where things stay safe even with nobody watching. An open field is not secured. The owner's standing beside it is what guards it, and that lets it acquire. So שמואל and רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא do not conflict.

keyTerms.meaning: 'These words apply only to...', a phrase that limits a rule
A guarded courtyard, where items stay safe with no one watching
An unguarded courtyard, like an open field
Yes / no

steps.whatToRemember: A guarded חצר acquires for its owner even without his knowledge. An unguarded חצר, like an open field, acquires only when the owner stands next to it, because his presence is what guards it.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not arguing with רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא. Both are right. Each one is talking about a different kind of courtyard.
steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between a guarded and an unguarded חצר is a basic rule of קנין חצר that comes up again and again in the סוגיות that follow.

phrases.english: These words apply only to a guarded courtyard,
but a courtyard that is not guarded,
if he is standing next to his field, yes, it acquires,
and if not, it does not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by limiting רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's rule to a guarded courtyard.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the cited rule applies to a guarded courtyard, while שמואל's condition applies to an unguarded one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any חצר, even an open field, acquires for its owner without his presence or knowledge.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a guarded חצר acquires on its own. An unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands beside it.

steps.title: Asking for a source for the unguarded-field rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that an unguarded חצר acquires only when the owner stands beside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know that a courtyard that is not guarded acquires for its owner if he stands beside his field, and does not acquire if he is not there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for the answer it just gave in Step 7. It is setting up the next move, where it will bring a ברייתא as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 7 the גמרא split the cases into two. A guarded חצר acquires even without the owner's knowledge. An unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands next to it. Now the גמרא wants an earlier source that shows this distinction is real and not just invented to answer the question.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do you say this? (a request for a source)
A courtyard (property) that is not guarded
Yes

phrases.english: And from where do you say
that a courtyard that is not guarded,
if he is standing beside his field, yes, it acquires,
and if not, it does not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the distinction given as the answer in Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source proving that an unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands beside it.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a forgotten sheaf
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא discusses an owner in town who knows his workers forgot a sheaf. The פסוק teaches that the rule of forgetting applies in the field, not in town.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: An owner was standing in town and said, 'I know my workers forgot a sheaf of mine in the field. It will not become שכחה, because I remember it.' One might think it is not שכחה. The פסוק says, 'and you forgot a sheaf in the field.' This teaches that forgetting counts in the field, and not in town.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about שכחה as its source. The ברייתא's wording is confusing, and the גמרא will untangle it in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a sheaf the owner forgets in the field must be left for the poor. Here the owner remembered the sheaf while he was in town, and the question is what happens if he later forgets it. The פסוק's words 'in the field' will turn out to be the key to the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
A forgotten sheaf, which must be left for the poor
A sheaf of grain
One might have thought
The פסוק teaches (to correct that thought)

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא:
He was standing in the town and saying,
"I know that a sheaf that I have in the field
the workers forgot it,
so it shall not be a forgotten sheaf"
One might think it is not a forgotten sheaf,
phrases.notes: This is talking about a case where he later forgot it himself.

phrases.english: so the verse teaches: "and you forgot a sheaf in the field,"
"in the field … and you forgot": and not in the town.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source requested in Step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The distinction that an unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands beside it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on שכחה, built on דברים 24:19.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: The opening of the ברייתא implies the sheaf is שכחה, but the פסוק it quotes seems to say it is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא itself is difficult. You said 'one might think it is not שכחה,' so the answer must be that it is שכחה. Then it brings the teaching 'in the field, and not in town,' which sounds like it is not שכחה!
steps.whatsHappening: Before using the ברייתא as proof, the גמרא points out that its own words seem to clash.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'One might think it is not' means the conclusion is that it IS שכחה. But 'in the field, not in town' sounds like a sheaf forgotten in town is NOT שכחה. Both cannot be true unless the ברייתא is read differently.

keyTerms.meaning: This source itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)
Apparently / this shows that
It brings the teaching from the פסוק

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said, "one might think it is not a forgotten sheaf,"
so apparently it is a forgotten sheaf,
and then it brings the teaching
"in the field … and you forgot," and not in the town,
so apparently it is not a forgotten sheaf!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out an internal contradiction in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'one might think' wording implies it is שכחה, but the derived teaching 'not in town' implies it is not.

steps.title: Rereading the ברייתא: standing in the field makes it his חצר
steps.stepSummary: In the field, a sheaf remembered and later forgotten is not שכחה, because his field acquired it while he stood there. In town, the field does not acquire for him, so it is שכחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what the ברייתא means. In the field, a sheaf forgotten from the start is שכחה, but a sheaf remembered and later forgotten is not. Why? Because he is standing beside it, the field counts as his חצר and acquires the sheaf for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction with a new reading of the ברייתא. That reading turns out to prove the rule of שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'in the field, not in town' teach a difference. In the field, once the owner remembers the sheaf, his field acquires it, because he is standing next to it. So it can no longer become שכחה. In town he is not standing there, so the field does not acquire, and if he later forgets the sheaf it is שכחה. This shows an unguarded field acquires only when the owner is beside it.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't this what it means?
Forgotten from the very start
Remembered at first, then forgotten in the end
It acquired for him

steps.whatToRemember: An unguarded field acquires for its owner only while he stands beside it. That is why a sheaf he remembered in the field is no longer שכחה, but one he remembered only in town still can be.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Not in town' does not mean a sheaf remembered in town can never be שכחה. It means the special protection, where the field acquires the sheaf for him, works only when he is standing in the field.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the proof for שמואל's limit on the משנה. It also shows that the rule of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (acquiring without knowing) is limited to a guarded חצר.

phrases.english: Rather, isn't this what it is saying:
In the field, a sheaf forgotten from the start is a forgotten sheaf,
but one remembered and in the end forgotten is not a forgotten sheaf.
What is the reason?
Because since he is standing beside it,
it counts as his courtyard, and it acquired the sheaf for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from Step 10, and in doing so completes the proof asked for in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source as a distinction between the owner being in the field and being in town.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say, at the same time, that the sheaf is and is not שכחה.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the field, a remembered sheaf is acquired by his field because he stands there, so it is not שכחה. In town there is no acquisition, so it is שכחה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands beside it, which supports שמואל.

steps.title: In town the sheaf is forgotten because the owner is not next to his field
steps.stepSummary: In town, even a sheaf that was remembered and then forgotten counts as שכחה, because the owner is not near his field, so it cannot acquire for him. This proves that an unguarded field acquires only when the owner stands beside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But in town, even if the sheaf was remembered and in the end forgotten, it is שכחה. Why? Because he is not next to it so that his field could acquire it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the town half of its explanation and gives the reason: the owner is not next to his field. This reason is the proof we were looking for in step 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the field, the owner's field already acquired the sheaf while he was remembering it, so forgetting it later does not matter. In town, the field could not acquire it, because he was not standing there. So the only difference between field and town is whether the owner is standing next to his field, and that proves an unguarded field acquires only with the owner beside it.

keyTerms.meaning: In town (the owner is away from his field)
Remembered at first, and forgotten in the end
What is the reason?
So that it (the field) can acquire for him

steps.whatToRemember: An unguarded field acquires for its owner only when he is standing next to it. That is why a sheaf forgotten while he is in town counts as שכחה.

phrases.english: But in town,
even if it was remembered and in the end forgotten,
it is a forgotten sheaf.
What is the reason?
Because he is not next to it, so that it could acquire for him.
phrases.notes: 'It' here is his field: since he isn't standing there, the field can't acquire the sheaf for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא – דְּלֵיתֵיהּ גַּבֵּיהּ דְּלִזְכֵּי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the town half of the תירוץ in step 11 and turns it into the proof for the question in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: An unguarded field acquires for its owner only when he stands beside it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about an owner in town whose workers forgot a sheaf, as explained in step 11.

steps.title: Maybe the field and town difference is just a Torah decree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: maybe the Torah simply decreed that forgetting in the field counts as שכחה and forgetting in town does not, with no connection to acquiring.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know? Maybe it is a decree of the פסוק that in the field it is שכחה and in town it is not שכחה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the proof from step 12. Maybe the difference between field and town has nothing to do with the field acquiring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on explaining the ברייתא through the rules of acquiring. But the פסוק says 'בַּשָּׂדֶה' (in the field), so maybe the Torah simply limited שכחה to the field as a rule, a גזירת הכתוב. If so, the ברייתא teaches nothing about how a field acquires.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you know? (a challenge to a proof)
Perhaps
A decree of the פסוק: a rule with no reason given beyond the פסוק itself

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the ברייתא's own reading. The ברייתא said in town it is שכחה; this suggestion reads the פסוק simply, that only the field counts and the town does not.

phrases.english: From where do you know?
Perhaps it is a decree of the פסוק,
that in the field it is a forgotten sheaf
and in town it is not a forgotten sheaf!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof drawn in step 12 by offering a different explanation of the field and town difference.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof that an unguarded field acquires only with the owner beside it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The field and town difference could come from a plain Torah decree limiting שכחה to the field, not from rules of acquiring.

steps.title: The פסוק includes sheaves forgotten in town
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the words 'לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ' include forgetting in town, so there is no Torah decree excluding the town.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Do not go back to take it.' This comes to include a sheaf forgotten in town.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its proof against step 13. It brings a phrase from the פסוק showing that forgetting in town also counts as שכחה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah includes the town in the law of שכחה, then the town is not excluded by decree. So when a remembered-then-forgotten sheaf is not שכחה in the field, the reason must be acquiring: the field acquires only when the owner stands there.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק says
Do not go back to take it
To include (an extra case)

phrases.english: The פסוק says:
"Do not go back to take it,"
to include forgetting in town.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: לֹא תָּשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ, לְרַבּוֹת שִׁכְחַת הָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the דחיה of step 13 and brings back the proof of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a separate phrase in the פסוק that includes the town case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Torah may have simply excluded the town from שכחה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Town forgetting is included, so the field and town difference must come from the rules of acquiring.

steps.title: That phrase is needed for the prohibition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the phrase 'לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ' is needed to create a לאו against taking a forgotten sheaf, so it cannot also include the town.
steps.simpleTranslation: This phrase is needed for the prohibition!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 14. The phrase it used is already busy teaching something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A phrase can teach an extra case only if it is not needed for its plain meaning. Here the plain meaning is a לאו: one who forgot a sheaf may not go back and take it. So the phrase has no room to also include the town, and the proof is in trouble again.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for (a different teaching)
A Torah prohibition (a 'do not' commandment)

phrases.english: This is needed for the prohibition!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source used in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of 'לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ' to include forgetting in town.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase is needed for its plain meaning, the לאו against taking a forgotten sheaf, so it is not extra and cannot teach an added case.

steps.title: The extra words 'do not go back' include forgetting in town
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that if the פסוק only wanted a לאו against taking the sheaf, it could have said 'לֹא תִּקָּחֶנּוּ'. The longer wording 'לֹא תָשׁוּב' adds the town case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the פסוק should have just said 'You shall not take it.' Why does it say 'You shall not go back'? To include a sheaf forgotten while the owner is in town.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 15. The פסוק could have made the לאו with a shorter phrase, so the words 'go back' must be teaching something extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the words 'לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ' are used up by the לאו. Here the גמרא points out that 'לֹא תִּקָּחֶנּוּ' would have been enough for the לאו. So the word 'תָשׁוּב' is extra, and it is used to include שכחה in town.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if your explanation is right
You shall not take it, a shorter wording the פסוק could have used
To include an extra case
A sheaf forgotten while the owner is in town

phrases.english: If so,
let the verse say: 'You shall not take it.'
Why does it say 'You shall not go back'?
To include forgetting in town.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15 by showing that the wording of the פסוק is longer than the לאו needs.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording: the פסוק uses more words than the לאו needs, so the extra word teaches an additional case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole phrase 'לֹא תָשׁוּב לְקַחְתּוֹ' is needed for the לאו, so nothing is left over to include the town.
steps.terutzMaskana: A shorter phrase would have made the לאו, so 'תָשׁוּב' is free to include שכחה in town.

steps.title: The words 'do not go back' are needed for the front-and-behind rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that 'לֹא תָשׁוּב' is still needed for a משנה's rule: a sheaf in front of the owner is not שכחה, and a sheaf behind him is.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the phrase is still needed for what we learned in a משנה: a sheaf in front of him is not שכחה, and a sheaf behind him is שכחה, because it falls under 'do not go back.' This is the rule: any sheaf that falls under 'do not go back' is שכחה, and any sheaf that does not is not שכחה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 16. It says the word 'go back' already has a job, so it cannot also teach the town case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה uses the word 'תָשׁוּב' to define which sheaves can become שכחה. Only a sheaf the owner has already passed, so that he would have to turn back to get it, counts. A sheaf still ahead of him does not. Since the word is used for this rule, it is not extra, and the town case again has no source.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is still needed for something else
For what we learned in a משנה
A sheaf in front of him that he has not reached yet
A sheaf behind him that he has already passed
The prohibition 'do not go back'
This is the general rule

steps.confusionAlert: 'In front' and 'behind' here are about where the owner is while he collects sheaves in the field. This is a different question from field versus town.

phrases.english: But it is still needed
for that which we learned in a Mishnah:
a sheaf in front of him is not a forgotten sheaf,
a sheaf behind him is a forgotten sheaf,
because it falls under 'You shall not go back.'
This is the rule:
any sheaf that falls under 'You shall not go back' is a forgotten sheaf,

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּבַל תָּשׁוּב – אֵינוֹ שִׁכְחָה!
phrases.english: any sheaf that does not fall under 'You shall not go back' is not a forgotten sheaf!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 16 by showing that the 'extra' word already has another use.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 16 that 'לֹא תָשׁוּב' is extra and includes שכחה in town.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה uses 'תָשׁוּב' to teach that only sheaves behind the owner become שכחה. Since the word is already used, it cannot also include the town case.

steps.title: רב אשי learns the town case from the word 'it shall be'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the town case comes from a different word in the פסוק, 'יִהְיֶה'. So the Torah does include forgetting in town, and the original proof stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The פסוק says 'it shall be.' That word includes a sheaf forgotten while the owner is in town.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the challenge from step 17. He finds a new word in the פסוק that includes the town case, so 'לֹא תָשׁוּב' can stay with its job in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'יִהְיֶה' including the town case, the idea from step 13 falls away. That idea was that the Torah simply left out the town case. Since the Torah does include it, the difference between field and town must come from acquiring. This brings back the proof of step 12: an unguarded field acquires for its owner only when he stands beside it.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the final answer here
The פסוק says; introduces a source from the wording
'It shall be' (דברים 24:19), used here to include the town case

steps.whatToRemember: The Torah includes forgetting in town through the word 'יִהְיֶה'. So the only reason a remembered-then-forgotten sheaf in the field is not שכחה is that the field acquired it while the owner stood there. This confirms that an unguarded field acquires only when the owner is beside it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the defense of the proof from step 12. It supports the rule that a person's field can acquire for him only when he stands next to it.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
The verse says 'it shall be'
to include forgetting in town.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17 by finding a different word in the פסוק for the town case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New source: a different word in the same פסוק teaches the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With 'לֹא תָשׁוּב' used up, there is no source for the town case, so maybe the Torah simply left it out.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'יִהְיֶה' includes the town case, so the field-versus-town difference must come from acquiring, and the proof of step 12 stands.

steps.title: Two more אמוראים agree: the owner must be standing next to his field
steps.stepSummary: עולא and רבה בר בר חנה both say the same condition: a field acquires for its owner only when he is standing next to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And עולא said the same thing: this rule works only when the owner is standing next to his field. And רבה בר בר חנה said the same thing too: only when he is standing next to his field.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the side-discussion is over, the גמרא goes back to the main condition. It tells us that עולא and רבה בר בר חנה also hold that the owner must be standing beside his field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the law here. The point is that this condition is not one lone opinion, because two more אמוראים say it word for word. This also sets up the next step, where רבי אבא challenges עולא by name.

keyTerms.meaning: And so said: introduces another scholar who says the same thing
עולא, an אמורא who often brought teachings from ארץ ישראל to בבל
רבה בר בר חנה, an אמורא
Next to his field

phrases.english: And so said עולא:
Only where he is standing next to his field.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה:
phrases.english: And so said רבה בר בר חנה:
Only where he is standing next to his field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the שכחה side-discussion ends in Step 18, the גמרא returns to the main condition and brings two more אמוראים who hold it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person's field acquires a found object for him only when he is standing next to the field. עולא and רבה בר בר חנה both hold this.

steps.title: רבי אבא challenges עולא from רבן גמליאל on the ship
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא starts a challenge against עולא from a story: רבן גמליאל, traveling on a ship, gave a tenth of his produce to רבי יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא raised a challenge against עולא from this teaching: There was a story about רבן גמליאל and the זקנים, who were traveling on a ship. רבן גמליאל said: The tenth that I will measure out in the future is given to יהושע,
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא starts a challenge against עולא by quoting a story. This section ends in the middle of the story, so here the גמרא is only setting up the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story, everyone is far out at sea, nowhere near the produce. Even so, רבן גמליאל gives a tithe from it to יהושע. The challenge to עולא depends on how the person receiving it gets ownership while he is not standing next to the produce. The rest of the story, coming next, explains this and completes the challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him: an objection brought from an earlier teaching such as a משנה or ברייתא
A story, an event that really happened
The elders, meaning the leading חכמים
A ship
A tenth, meaning the tithe (מעשר)
To measure out

steps.confusionAlert: The quote is not finished here. Do not try to figure out the full challenge yet. The rest of the story, which comes next, shows how the tithe actually reached the people it was given to.

phrases.english: רבי אבא raised a challenge against עולא:
There was a story about רבן גמליאל and the elders
who were traveling on a ship.
רבן גמליאל said:
The tenth that I am going to measure out in the future
is given to יהושע,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהושע. The tithe goes to him because he is a לוי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 19 named עולא as holding the 'standing next to his field' condition. Now רבי אבא challenges him directly.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's rule that a field acquires for its owner only when he is standing next to it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everyone was far away on a ship, yet רבן גמליאל gave a tithe from his produce to יהושע. The rest of the story will show how יהושע acquired it from a distance, without standing next to the property. That would contradict עולא's condition. The challenge is finished in the next part of the story.
